outline.description: This chapter introduces the parties, the premium financing arrangement, the underlying facts giving rise to the lawsuit, and the procedural journey from state court to the Fifth Circuit. It explains how Williams, Wright, and Jenkins financed their GoAuto policies through APAC, how their policies were cancelled for nonpayment, and how the class action alleging ineffective cancellation and bad faith was removed to federal court and resolved on summary judgment.
subtopics: The parties: GoAuto Insurance, the insureds (Williams, Wright, Jenkins), and the premium finance company (APAC)
The premium financing arrangement: APAC pays full premium upfront, insureds pay APAC in installments, APAC holds power of attorney to cancel on default
The underlying accident involving Jenkins and the resulting class action lawsuit
Procedural history: filing in Louisiana state court, removal to federal court, cross-motions for summary judgment on statutory compliance
The district court's grant of GoAuto's summary judgment motion and dismissal of all claims with prejudice
The scope of the appeal: three contentions regarding delivery of notice, receipt of cancellation requests, and denial of plaintiffs' motion

outline.chapter_title: Louisiana's Statutory Framework for Cancellation of Financed Insurance Policies
outline.description: This chapter sets out the governing Louisiana statute, La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3), and the strict adherence doctrine that Louisiana courts apply when a premium finance company exercises its power of attorney to cancel a policy. It also describes GoAuto's actual cancellation procedures, which form the basis for the statutory compliance analysis.
subtopics: The statutory mechanism: how a premium finance company requests cancellation by sending notice to the insurer
The four certification requirements under La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(a)(i)-(iv): valid power of attorney, uncured default, notice sent to insured, copies sent to interested parties
The strict adherence doctrine: Louisiana courts require strict compliance with statutory procedures
The dual purpose of strict adherence: fixing exact time of cancellation and providing minimum cure period (Britten v. Reavis)
Consequences of noncompliance: any defect renders cancellation ineffective (Eaglin v. Champion Ins. Co.)
GoAuto's cancellation procedures: APAC's ten-day notice, automated e-mail to GoAuto, certification language, automatic computer cancellation, post-cancellation signing and stamping
The pre-2017 vs. post-2017 procedures for handling cancellation documents

outline.chapter_title: The Signature Requirement: Does 'Certifying' Mean Signing?
outline.description: This chapter examines the plaintiffs' central argument that the statutory requirement of 'certifying' necessitates a signature on the cancellation notice before cancellation can occur. It analyzes the statutory text, relevant Louisiana case law, and the Fifth Circuit's conclusion that the statute does not require a signature when the company itself certifies the required information.
subtopics: Plaintiffs' argument: no signature exists on APAC's certification until after the policy is automatically cancelled
The statutory text: La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(a) makes no explicit reference to a signature
Whether the word 'certifying' implicitly requires a signature
Louisiana case law review: KMJ Services (requirement of 'statement certifying compliance'), Hodges (cancellation upon receipt of notice and statement), Lewis v. Julien (no signature discussion)
Benitez v. Elsayed: the one case mentioning lack of signature, but alongside other deficiencies; did not hold signature alone is disqualifying
Distinguishing Benitez: here, unlike in Benitez, each notice actually 'certifies' the relevant information
The court's reasoning: the statute identifies the 'insurance premium finance company' as the certifying entity, not a named individual
Conclusion: 'strict adherence' does not authorize courts to add requirements the legislature did not include; no signature required

outline.chapter_title: The Receipt Requirement: Did GoAuto Properly 'Receive' the Cancellation Request?
outline.description: This chapter addresses the plaintiffs' second argument: that GoAuto never properly 'received' the cancellation request because of the shared corporate infrastructure between GoAuto and APAC. It examines the statutory requirement of receipt, the definition of 'receipt,' the computerized cancellation process, and the court's conclusion that electronic receipt by GoAuto's computer system satisfies the statute.
subtopics: Plaintiffs' argument: pre-2017, the filing room belonged to GoAuto Management Services (not GoAuto); post-2017, the stamping employee is an APAC employee
Plaintiffs' interpretation: the legislature's use of 'receipt' (not just 'sending') requires GoAuto to take possession before cancelling
The statutory provision: La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i) - 'Upon receipt of such notice... the insurer shall consider that cancellation... has been requested'
The absence of a statutory definition of 'receipt' and no Louisiana Supreme Court guidance
Black's Law Dictionary definitions of 'receipt' (taking physical possession) and 'receive' (coming into possession from an outside source)
The computerized process: APAC's system calls a GoAuto web service that acts as a 'listener,' automatically processing cancellation requests
No human involvement until after the computer system effects cancellation
The court's conclusion: electronic receipt by GoAuto's computer system satisfies the statutory 'receipt' requirement
The district court's alternative reasoning: treating the APAC employee as a 'private carrier' - the Fifth Circuit declines to reach this issue

outline.chapter_title: Certification to the Louisiana Supreme Court and Disposition
outline.description: This chapter covers the plaintiffs' request that the Fifth Circuit certify the unresolved questions of Louisiana statutory interpretation to the Louisiana Supreme Court. It explains the standard for certification, the court's reasoning for declining, and the final disposition of the case.
subtopics: Plaintiffs' request for certification: arguing the issues are important to Louisiana's insurance industry and statutory scheme
The Fifth Circuit's general posture on certification: chary about certifying absent compelling reason (Jefferson v. Lead Industry Ass'n)
The principle that lack of state supreme court definition is insufficient to warrant certification
The court's decline to certify the questions
Final disposition: GoAuto's procedures comply with the statute, district court did not err in denying plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment
The court's affirmance of the district court's dismissal of all claims with prejudice
